Juan Soto has been around the big leagues for long enough to almost forget just how young he is.
Soto is in his ninth big league season, and yet he is somehow still just 27 years old. In comparison, New York Mets rookie starter Nolan McLean is 25 years old, and that's not a wild number, by any means. Soto is an anomaly, and it's why the Mets handed him a mammoth 15-year, $765 million deal ahead of the 2025 season.
With the Mets struggling throughout the season, Soto's greatness likely hasn't been talked about as much as it probably should. But this guy is special. One stat that jumps out is the fact that he's one of just five players in big league history with 250 or more homers and more walks than strikeouts before his 28th birthday, along with Albert Pujols, Mel Ott, Eddie Mathews and Jimmie Foxx, as shared on X by RotoBaller's Eric Cross.
Juan Soto Is Putting Himself Up There With The Greats
That's three Hall of Famers and Pujols, who will be in the second that he's eligible. If Soto can keep this up, he's well on his way as well.
On Thursday, Soto went 0-for-3 with a walk. For his career, Soto has 271 long balls and 972 walks, to just 897 strikeouts in 1,204 games played. He's not going to turn 28 years old until October 25. On the season, the young superstar is slashing .274/.393/.522 with 27 homers and 68 RBIs in 108 games played. The only thing that has slowed him down this season is injuries, and yet he has still had a good overall season. Over the last two seasons, he hit over 40 homers and drove in over 100 runs in at least 157 games. His numbers so far this season are on pace with his last few, if he didn't get hurt.
There are few guys in big league history who have been able to start a career like Soto has. He's a five-time All-Star, six-time Silver Slugger Award winner, one-time batting champ, one-time Home Run Derby champ and a World Series champion. And, again, he's just 27 years old. He should just get better.
He's already etched his name onto plenty of historic lists and the scary thing is the fact that realistically, we may not have seen his best yet. Theoretically, he should be just starting to enter his prime, and yet he's already historic.

item.content:encoded:
Greatest is something every player who wears a New York Mets uniform strives for. Many come and go and are either forgotten about entirely or stick somewhere in the franchise’s lore for having one amazing moment. Fans know Mike Baxter for saving Johan Santana’s no-hitter. They’ll recall the name Mackey Sasser for the inability to throw the ball back to the pitcher safely. Kirk Nieuwenhuis had his random 3-home run game. Luis Castillo lives on in infamy for dropping a routine pop up at Yankee Stadium to end the night.
A mix of greatness and defeat have followed the Mets since they were officially born for the 1962 MLB season. Several Hall of Famers have come through to call the Polo Grounds, Shea Stadium, and Citi Field home. Everything from a mix of the homegrown talent of Tom Seaver to the ill-fated signing of Justin Verlander have a part in Mets history.
While some players live on forever with statues or their numbers retired, so do individual seasons. Random, expected, and in other seasons a longtime coming, these 25 individual seasons by Mets players are the greatest in the franchise’s history. You can’t think of these players without recalling how impressive of a year they had.
The 25 best seasons by Mets players in franchise history
25) Gary Carter, 1985
Gary Carter’s entrance into Mets lore began with a bang. Literally. He homered on Opening Day 1985 and would continue to pummel baseballs throughout the season for his new ball club. Carter finished with a 6.9 bWAR (what does that mean in 1985?) plus 32 home runs and 100 RBI. Exactly matching the .853 OPS he had in his final year with the Montreal Expos the year prior, it was the early telltale sign the Mets made the right decision to make him a part of their core. Partly because the Mets made the playoffs the next year, Carter was able to jump from sixth to third in the MVP vote. Despite this, his 1985 season was the better one.
24) Cleon Jones, 1969
Offense isn’t what won the Mets the 1969 World Series. The hitting was okay, but for the longest time, Cleon Jones’ .340 batting average sat well above anyone else in franchise history. Worth 7 bWAR in part because of an atypical season where he actually rated positively as a defender, Jones had an often-overlooked year where he finished 7th in the NL MVP vote. In an era when pitching dominated, Jones’ season deserves more credit. The year might not compare as well as some Mets years with 30+ home runs or 100+. However, for the timing of when it took place and the well-aged batting average, Jones deserves the accolades.
23) Jesse Orosco, 1983
Spoiler alert! There won’t be another relief pitcher on this list. They’re sometimes hard to judge because of how many fewer innings they throw. Plus, with the ever-evolving usage of arms, they don’t stack up well against each other in different eras. Nevertheless, what Jesse Orosco accomplished in 1983 was outlandish. At 13-7 all out of the bullpen, he tossed 110 innings and had a 1.47 ERA. The effort earned him third place in the NL Cy Young. It was a one-of-a-kind type of season from a Mets reliever. Somewhat unspoken, it was only his second full season as a major league pitcher and already he was at the top of his game while helping to further define the closer role.
22) Jose Reyes, 2006
Several different Jose Reyes seasons deserve to be on this list. How does one differentiate between them? He won a batting title in 2011 but lacked in other areas. In 2006, he hit .300, had a career-best 5.9 bWAR, and stole 64 bases. Most memorable was scoring 122 runs and driving in another 81. Homering 19 times helped make this maybe his most prolific offensive season for New York. The 2006 Mets are remembered for their incredible lineup. Reyes at the very top was one of the biggest factors.
21) Edgardo Alfonzo, 2000
Edgardo Alfonzo is a beloved Mets player. He crosses off a lot of the boxes fans desire. He was homegrown, versatile, and put together some really good years for winning ball clubs. In 2000, he wasn’t the main attraction and yet the season’s totals hold up nicely all of these years later. His lone All-Star season included a career-best 6.4 bWAR with 25 home runs and 94 RBI. Both of those numbers were a little short of what he did the year previous. However, his .967 OPS overpowered any of his past seasons and remains one of the best in Mets history. Alfonzo could be trusted to hit anywhere from first to fifth in the lineup if needed.
20) Lance Johnson, 1996
The 1996 Mets weren’t very good, but they did have three players who hit really well. One of the trio put together a season that landed him on the record books and doesn’t look like it’ll be surpassed. Lance Johnson’s 227 hits and 21 triples both set single-season Mets records while leading the league. In addition to the bat, he stole 50 bases and earned himself a 1.9 dWAR. If we were ranking only seasons by Mets leadoff hitters, this would be right near the top. It’s a shame this couldn’t have occurred on a better season for the team.
19) Jerry Koosman, 1968
Jerry Koosman did something amazing. By many measurements, his best year was his first. Koosman had a small sampling in the majors during the 1967 season. The following year qualified as his rookie campaign. Koosman went 19-12 with a 2.08 ERA. He’d end up 13th in the Cy Young race and the runner-up for the Rookie of the Year, just barely, when Johnny Bench beat him for the honor. A coin toss might have been the decider for some voters as both NL rookies had a case. Koosman was later the Cy Young runner-up in 1976. Compared to 1968, his freshman year was the better of the two.
18) David Cone, 1988
Who says wins don’t matter? In 1988, David Cone went a remarkable 20-3. He wasn’t vulturing wins thanks to the help of a strong offense. Cone pitched to a 2.22 ERA while finishing third in the Cy Young race and 10th in the MVP vote. A somewhat underrated pitcher whose career spanned the lighter hitting 1980s through the Steroid Era of the 1990s, this first full season in a Mets uniform was a preview of the strikeout machine he’d later become. Fanning 212, he’d later manage to lead the league in 1990 and 1991. The ERA in 1988 was about a full run better making this the more worthy campaign.
17) Pete Alonso, 2019
Pete Alonso posted some of the most unique statistics in Mets history. The power is unmatched in a single season and career. His rookie season in 2019 featuring 53 home runs and 120 RBI also included a 5.4 bWAR and a career-high .941 OPS. The record-setting debut season out of Alonso was more than enough to make a lasting impression on Mets fans who will never stop loving him. Alonso, like some others on this list, gets bonus points for doing it as a rookie. Those 53 home runs will be tough for a veteran, let alone a player with no MLB experience, to ever match. He became the Mets home run king for a reason. His power is unmatched from just the eye test.
16) Juan Soto, 2025
Statistically impressive, the only thing missing from Juan Soto’s first year with the Mets was purpose. The team collapsed late despite Soto putting together yet another one of his token MVP-caliber seasons. Along with hitting 43 home runs and posting a league-high .396 OBP, Soto stole 38 bases. His previous single-season high was 12. Truly a one-of-a-kind type of year, the only reason this isn’t higher is because the defense slowed him down. It was the type of year to build off of while making his record-setting contract worth it to Steve Cohen.
15) Francisco Lindor, 2024
Francisco Lindor’s MVP runner-up season in 2024 needs to be experienced to fully understand. He started off as poorly as the team and managed to quite literally lead the club to the NLCS. His first 30/30 season which includes his time in Cleveland was far more complicated than just looking at the .844 OPS. Lindor was a leader and with another Gold Glove-caliber season at shortstop, managed to put together a 6.8 bWAR season. Nothing about the season was statistically insane yet Lindor seemed to do a little bit of everything well.
14) Darryl Strawberry, 1987
Strangely, the best season of Darryl Strawberry’s career with the Mets took place in a non-playoff campaign. The 1987 Mets were good, but not good enough. Strawberry set new career highs with 39 home runs and 104 RBI. Slashing .284/.398/.583 with 36 stolen bases, it was maybe the most complete year Strawberry had as an offensive player. Although he’d lead the league in multiple offensive categories in 1988, many of his 1987 totals were superior. Crossing 30 home runs and 100 RBI for the first time in his career, it was a bit of a transition from Strawberry being one of the star players to be the signature member of the Mets.
13) Bernard Gilkey, 1996
Mets fans who weren’t familiar with Bernard Gilkey’s work might assume he was always one of the better middle of the order hitters. Arriving via trade with the St. Louis Cardinals prior to the 1996 season, Gilkey cranked it up to a whole new level. It feels appropriate that he’d later make a cameo in Men in Black because Gilkey’s numbers were unworldly. He slashed .317/.393/.562 with 44 doubles, 30 home runs, and 117 RBI. The doubles are still the most of any Mets player in a single-season. The 8.1 bWAR became the best in Mets history by a position player. Created by both his bat and glove, Gilkey led the league with 18 assists, 4 double plays, 309 putouts, and ranked as the best at his position in range factor.
12) Tom Seaver, 1975
You knew Tom Seaver was coming eventually. His 1975 season earned him his third and final Cy Young Award. He probably could have had more. This season was a 7.8 bWAR campaign that had him going 22-9 with a 2.38 ERA and a league-leading 243 strikeouts. Compared to most players, it’s incredible. On the list of Seaver performances, this one is easy to overlook because even one of his non-Cy Young winning years was better. Don’t worry. Tom Terrific is all over this list with several seasons that were even better.
11) Tom Seaver, 1969
When it comes to Mets greatness, Tom Seaver is the “you haven’t seen the last of me!” in franchise history. The 1969 season ended with a championship for the Mets. In the regular season, Seaver won a franchise-record 25 games while on his way to his first Cy Young and an MVP runner-up. Neither the 2.21 ERA nor 208 strikeouts would set personal bests. This might have been the most rewarding individual season of Seaver’s career yet it falls short of his best by quite a couple. At least he got winning the big one out of the way relatively early.
10) Jacob deGrom, 2019
Speaking of Cy Young Mets seasons, Jacob deGrom got his second in 2019. His 7.2 bWAR led the league as did the 255 strikeouts. By this point, greatness was something Mets fans weren’t demanding from deGrom, it was expected. A good length away from some of those other memorable Mets seasons by pitchers like Tom Seaver, his 2.43 ERA doesn’t even do him justice for how dominant he was for his second straight season as the best pitcher in the sport. Sadly, this would end up as his final full season in a Mets uniform due to a pandemic as well as injuries in 2021 and 2022.
9) Mike Piazza, 2000
Mike Piazza had big years, moments, and numbers with the Mets. Because his defense behind the plate was never good, stats like WAR don’t rank quite as high as some others. The 2000 season was big regardless as Piazza hit .324/.398/.614 with a 1.012 OPS. The OPS was the largest in any full season for a Mets player. The year included 38 home runs and 113 RBI with the real kicker being that he had only 482 at-bats. One of those more underrated qualities about his offensive abilities, he walked 58 times while only going down on strikes 69 times.
8) Howard Johnson, 1989
Howard Johnson led the league in home runs and RBI in 1991, but it was his 1989 season which deserves a spot on this list. Armed with 36 home runs and 101 RBI, Johnson’s speed went on display with 41 stolen bases. It was his second 30/30 season with the Mets. He hit .287 as well, atypical for the .251 he hit while in orange and blue. Never the biggest star on the Mets roster during his best years in the late 1980s and early 1990s, Johnson’s powerful and speedy 1989 campaign was a special one and the best representation of what he had to offer the ball club during his peak seasons.
7) John Olerud, 1998
Each of the three seasons John Olerud spent with the Mets was special in its own way. A franchise-leading .354 batting average helps break the tie. That’s what he hit in 1998, his middle season with the club. Posting a 7.6 bWAR as well, Olerud was the 12th place finisher in the MVP race during a season where you didn’t get much attention if you weren’t hitting home runs. He had 22 with 93 RBI. More like Keith Hernandez leveled up on offense, newer statistics that emphasis on base have helped this season age better. Olerud was never the best first baseman in the league. In Mets history, he’s right there as one of the stronger overall performers.
6) Carlos Beltran, 2006
Carlos Beltran overcame a rough first year with the Mets in 2005 to put together one of the all-time great ones in 2006. The 41 home runs hit by Todd Hundley in 1996 were matched by Beltran. Posting an 8.2 bWAR, he set a new single-season high in franchise history that would only get to enjoy one season at the top. Beltran slashed .275/.388/.594. He had 95 walks and only 99 strikeouts to practically cancel each other out. The only negative about his season was how it ended. The visual of striking out looking to end Game 7 of the NLCS remains one of the first fans often think about when his name or heartbreaking Mets moments are mentioned.
5) David Wright, 2007
No Mets player has ever matched the popularity of David Wright. His 2007 season, an 8.3 bWAR campaign, set a new mark of excellence. This was Captain America at his absolute best. He hit 30 home runs, stole 34 bases, and cruised past 100 runs scored and RBI. He even hit .325 with a .416 OBP. To make sure no check boxes were left unfilled, he won a Silver Slugger and Gold Glove. The team’s collapse in 2007 likely had to do a lot with why he only finished fourth in the MVP.
4) Jacob deGrom, 2018
As much as Jacob deGrom’s ridiculously good 15-start season in 2021 was historic, it wasn’t a complete year. The 2018 season, on the other hand, included 32 starts and a magnificent 1.70 ERA. This was deGrom’s true coming out party. The debate all year was whether or not a pitcher with a losing record could win the Cy Young. He finished at 10-9 to void the conversation and was one vote shy of a unanimous decision for his first time winning the award. The season included multiple highs for deGrom including 269 strikeouts. It was the ultimate one-man army type of season in Mets history where the team was, oftentimes, only worth watching every fifth day.
3) Tom Seaver, 1971
Here’s the most ridiculous detail about the 1971 season for Tom Seaver: he didn’t win the Cy Young. A league-leading 10.2 bWAR wouldn’t have been known at the time, but a 20-10 record and league-best 1.76 ERA as well as 289 strikeouts to overtake every other pitcher in the National League should have been enough. Seaver settled as the runner-up to Ferguson Jenkins who had a 2.77 ERA and a 24-13 record. The race wasn’t even all that close with Jenkins getting 17 first-place votes and Seaver receiving 6. Both the Mets and Chicago Cubs won 83 games so it’s not as if team record mattered at all. In practically any other year, Seaver would have added more hardware to his collection.
2) Tom Seaver, 1973
If you crave Tom Seaver content, you’re in the right place. His 1973 season earned him his second Cy Young. He had a career-best 10.6 bWAR featuring a league-high 2.08 ERA, 18 complete games, and 251 strikeouts. The Mets would sneak into the postseason and then overtake the Big Red Machine Cincinnati Reds on their way to the World Series. The Mets fell short, of course, but the regular season showing by Seaver was valuable at cementing his Hall of Fame legacy. We can even include the playoffs if there was any doubt. Although he was 1-2 overall, he pitched to a 1.62 ERA in the NLCS and had a 2.40 ERA in the World Series. All the Mets were missing was league-average offense to win another championship.
1) Dwight Gooden, 1985
There shouldn’t have been any question as to what the best season by a Mets player was going to be because what Dwight Gooden did in 1985 was one of the greatest in MLB history. The 12.2 bWAR ranks as the 26th best in MLB history. It’s the best after 1913. Gooden went 24-4 with a 1.53 ERA. He led the league in complete games, innings, and struck out 268 batters. Those numbers matter a lot, as does one other one. Gooden was only 20-years-old for the entire season. This is the kind of year that’ll go unmatched by a Mets player until some sort of cosmic shift in the way the game is played or with the rule book. You can safely etch this into stone as the best.
Hall of Famers, players with retired numbers, some completely random yet memorable performances, and even a few active members cracked the list of the best individual Mets player seasons. Records were broken. Memories were made. In a couple of cases, championships were won.

(Photo credit: Raymond Carlin III)
Marcus Semien damaged his former team's playoff hopes Wednesday night when he hit a tie-breaking solo homer in the eighth inning to help the visiting New York Mets defeat the Texas Rangers, 7-2, in the middle game of a three-game interleague series.
Rangers closer Jacob Latz (3-4), pressed into a tie game prior with American League West co-leading Texas in borderline must-win mode, wriggled out of a bases loaded jam in the seventh and retired the first two batters of the eighth before Semien launched a 388-foot homer to left.
The homer was the first since Aug. 7 for Semien, who was dealt to the Mets in exchange for Brandon Nimmo last November.
New York's Juan Soto hit a two-run homer in the third and Brett Baty added insurance with a pinch-hit grand slam in the ninth for the Mets (73-85), who have won the first two games of the set.
Jake Burger had an RBI single in the fifth three batters before Evan Carter drove in the tying run by beating out the back end of a potential double play ball for the Rangers (78-80).
Texas entered play on Wednesday tied atop the American League West with the Houston Astros.
The Astros, who face the Seattle Mariners later Wednesday night, won the season series 9-4, which means Texas must win the division outright.
No baseball team has ever made the playoffs with a .500 or worse record in a full season.
Nolan McLean (12-10) capped an impressive rookie season by earning the win after allowing two runs on three hits and one walk, while striking out five over seven innings. McLean finished with a 3.16 ERA and 194 strikeouts over 31 starts and 179 2/3 innings.
Devin Williams, who was activated from the injured list Tuesday after missing seven weeks with a strained right shoulder, tossed a perfect eighth inning before Cionel Perez allowed one hit in the ninth.
Rangers starter Cody Bradford gave up two runs on four hits and no walks while striking out one over 4 1/3 innings.

item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON, Texas (AP) — Marcus Semien hit a tiebreaking homer in the eighth inning against his former team and Brett Baty added a pinch-hit grand slam in the ninth as the New York Mets beat the Texas Rangers 7-2 on Wednesday night.



























Rookie right-hander Nolan McLean (12-10) allowed two runs and three hits over seven innings for the last-place Mets (73-85), who have won both games in Texas since ex-interim manager Andy Green was given the full-time position Tuesday.









































The Rangers (78-80) have lost three consecutive games and trail first-place Houston by a half-game in the AL West, with the Astros playing later in Seattle. They own the head-to-head tiebreaker over Texas if the teams finish with the same record.



























Semien, traded by the Rangers to the Mets last November for Brandon Nimmo, launched his 15th homer this season off All-Star closer Jacob Latz (3-4) to give New York a 3-2 lead. Semien’s first homer since Aug. 7 snapped an 0-for-13 slump.



























Latz entered with two on and one out in the seventh, the first time he’s appeared before the eighth inning since April 12.












The Mets took a 2-0 lead in the third when Juan Soto followed Francisco Lindor’s two-out single with his 27th home run off starter Cody Bradford. It was Soto’s sixth homer this year against left-handed pitching.



























After that, Soto was intentionally walked three times — twice with runners on first and second and a left-hander on the mound.












Texas tied the score at 2 in the fifth after McLean retired the Rangers’ first 12 batters. Nimmo, who spent 10 seasons with the Mets, led off with a sharp single to right field. He advanced to second on Ezequiel Duran’s groundout and scored on Jake Burger’s single. Evan Carter drove in the tying run when he beat out a potential double-play grounder.



























New York left the bases loaded in the fifth and seventh after Soto was intentionally walked. He was given another free pass with first base open and two outs in the ninth, but Bo Bichette then walked against Trevor Williams to load the bases before Baty went deep.



























Rookie LHP Zac Thornton (5-5, 3.40 ERA) starts the series finale Thursday afternoon as the Mets look for a three-game sweep. Texas hadn't announced a scheduled starter.

KANSAS CITY, Mo. (AP) — Maikel Garcia had three hits and three RBIs, including a tiebreaking, run-scoring double in the seventh inning, as the Kansas City Royals beat the White Sox 5-4 Wednesday night and delayed Chicago's bid for a postseason berth.












Chicago could have secured its first playoff berth since 2021 with a win over the Royals and a Texas loss to the New York Mets.












Instead, Garcia and the Royals played the role of spoiler.












Connor Thomas (2-1) struck out one and allowed one hit in two scoreless innings for the win. Steven Cruz struck out two in the ninth and earned his eighth save.












Kansas City had three straight singles to open the bottom of the first and Garcia drove in two runs with a single to right. Vinnie Pasquantino followed with a double that scored Garcia. Pasquantino made it 4-0, scoring on shortstop Colson Montgomery’s throwing error.












Chicago opener Bryan Hudson recorded just one out while facing five batters and allowing four runs, three earned.












The White Sox responded with five hits in the third inning — including Kyle Teel’s two-run single and RBI hits by Miguel Vargas and Munetaka Murakami — sending 10 batters to the plate and tying the score at 4.












In his final start of the season, Kansas City's Seth Lugo allowed four runs on seven hits, striking out three in 3 1/3 innings. His 200 hits allowed lead the American League and his 99 earned runs allowed rank second.












Carter Jensen had three singles for the Royals (68-90), who snapped a five-game skid.












Braden Montgomery had three singles as the White Sox (81-77) remained one game behind the AL Central-leading Cleveland Guardians (82-76), who lost 1-0 to Boston.












Hagen Smith (3-3), the fourth of five Chicago pitchers, allowed a pair of hits and one run in the seventh.












The White Sox have not named a starter for Thursday's series finale. Royals RHP Randy Dobnak (3-4, 3.08 ERA) gets the start.

item.content:encoded:
Vladimir Guerrero Jr. has four games left before he can put his 2026 Toronto Blue Jays season behind him.
Guerrero, the six-time All-Star who signed the third highest-paid extension in MLB history in April 2025 at $500 million, has hit just nine home runs and slugged .359 to date for a career-low .695 OPS to date.
The Blue Jays, winners of the American League pennant this past season, where Guerrero was a major factor in reaching the World Series, were mathematically eliminated from this year’s postseason race as they hold a 77-81 record entering Wednesday.
This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.
For a player that is worth so much, especially financially, to an organization’s success, Guerrero’s down year has led to some vitriol from the Blue Jays’ fan base. And that’s likely to continue after hearing recent comments from the star infielder.
Guerrero, 27, sat down with Telemicro News recently, where he discussed his struggles at the plate this season, and how it reflects on his contract extension.
His comments were, well, interesting.
"The contract I got was based on what I did, not necessarily for what I’m going to do," Guerrero said, as translated by MLB reporter Héctor Gómez. "I understand why the fans believe it’s the other way around. Sometimes, I think that way, too, like, ‘Oh, they give me this money, and I’m not doing enough,’ but you know I try my best, and I’m working hard.
"The fans, I know how they are, when you are doing great they are 100% behind you. But when you are not at your best, not everybody is behind you, almost nobody supports you. Those are my real fans, the ones that are supporting me all the time."
After catching heat from Blue Jays fans, Guerrero was approached about the viral quotes, which he responded to.
"That was a quote from the interview when she asked me how I felt about this year," Guerrero said, via MLB.com. "I said that, obviously, I feel really bad about the year that I had, that I couldn’t help my team get to the postseason. I said I felt – that it’s my personal opinion – that every player gets paid for what they have done. With that said, you guys have got to remember that I signed my contract at the beginning of last year, then I did put up a good year. Then, the kind of playoffs that I had to help the team get into the World Series.
"To the fans, I’ve never stopped working very hard. I am going to go into the offseason again to prepare myself the best I can. Physically, mentally, everything that I have like I always do for my team and my teammates."
In Guerrero’s defense, that is technically what the Blue Jays did when they dished out his 14-year, $500 million extension, which is only behind Shohei Ohtani’s 10-year, $700 million deal with the Los Angeles Dodgers and Juan Soto’s 15-year, $765 million deal with the New York Mets. The franchise paid Guerrero for what he did from his debut in 2019 up to a fantastic 2025 campaign, where he belted eight homers and hit .397 across 18 postseason games.
But these comments show that Guerrero mustn’t be aware of what putting pen to money-filled paper meant in April 2025. No longer is it time in any sport, let alone Major League Baseball, where contracts are dished out based solely on past performance. It’s looking ahead to the future, where those past performances are expected to continue through a much-more lucrative deal.
MLB franchises sign players to contracts based on the market, and that market is justified by how the player will perform for them later on, while obviously looking at the track record in the past.
With any investment, those dishing out the big bucks want a return.
So, in a season where the home run total for a slugger is less than double digits – he still has time to at least get to 10 – and a career-low WAR (albeit the 2020 COVID-shortened campaign) has been accumulated, the Blue Jays and its fan base have every right to be disappointed. Yes, Guerrero was a major reason why Toronto reached the World Series in 2025, but the team and its fans are also allowed to voice displeasure with not just a down year – a career-worst performance in various metrics.
Would the Mets have dished out the highest-paying contract in league history if they didn’t expect Soto to continue performing at his superstar pace? No.
Would the Dodgers have agreed to give Ohtani $700 million, with heavy deferrals, might we add, to pay him for years without helping them reach their World Series goals? No.
From Mike Trout, to Mookie Betts, to Aaron Judge and the list goes on, every franchise wants to see a player they sign, especially for nine figures, to pay dividends. That’s the reality of the situation, whether Guerrero wants to view his deal as what he’s done in the past.
This is just one season, but Guerrero’s outlook needs to change just as much as his production moving forward on the remaining 13 years of his deal.

Max Scherzer has yet to reveal whether he plans to return for a 20th MLB season in 2027, but former teammate Juan Soto believes the Toronto Blue Jays veteran still has the competitive drive to keep pitching.
Scherzer, who is scheduled to make his 500th career MLB appearance Wednesday, recently declined to discuss his plans for next season. The 42-year-old has instead pointed to his ability to compete in meaningful games as the standard he uses to determine whether he should continue playing.
"You can give me a ball in a playoff start, and I can go out there and compete for it," Scherzer said last week, as reported by Brittany Ghiroli and Mitch Bannon of The Athletic. "That's my fundamental kind of litmus test of play or not play."
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
Soto, who played alongside Scherzer with the Washington Nationals and won the 2019 World Series with him, believes Scherzer's competitiveness continues to fuel him.
"I think he wants to play forever," Soto said, per Ghiroli and Bannon. "The love for the game he has, how confident he is. He's a guy who tries to win in every aspect, people don't even know, it's not even baseball. It's life.
"Everything with him is so competitive, and I think that's what drives him. It makes him go out there and try to show everybody he can still do it."
Scherzer has continued to adapt throughout the later stages of his career while maintaining a demanding workout routine between starts. His next appearance will add another milestone to a career that has included 499 games and 490 starts.
The right-hander enters Wednesday with a 224-125 career record, 3.28 ERA and 1.09 WHIP across 3,035 2/3 innings, according to datat from ESPN. He has recorded 3,543 strikeouts and 810 walks.
Scherzer has made 16 starts for Toronto this season, going 3-8 with a 6.07 ERA and 1.36 WHIP over 72 2/3 innings. He has struck out 54 and walked 31.
His most recent start provided a better result. Scherzer allowed one run on three hits over five innings in Toronto's 5-1 win over the Detroit Tigers on Sept. 16, earning his second win in four starts. He walked three and struck out three as the Blue Jays ended Detroit's six-game winning streak.

Field Level Media

23 Sep 2026, 12:25 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Brad Penner)
Drew Rasmussen allowed one hit in 6 2/3 outstanding innings and the visiting Tampa Bay Rays clinched the American League East with a 6-1 victory over the New York Yankees on Tuesday night in the nightcap of a day-night doubleheader.
The Rays won for the 20th time in 28 games and clinched their fifth division title. Tampa Bay last won the AL East in 2021 when it won a team-record 100 games. Yandy Diaz drove in four runs on a pair of singles.
Rasmussen (16-5) took a no-hitter into the seventh until Heliot Ramos opened the inning with a double to left for New York. Ramos eventually scored on an RBI single by rookie George Lombard Jr. off Kevin Kelly.
Rasmussen finished with 11 strikeouts for his fourth career double-digit strikeout performance. He finished two shy of his career-high set June 10 against the Boston Red Sox and the Rays won his 12th consecutive start.
Yankees 2, Rays 0 (Game 1)
Cody Bellinger hit a two-run home run in the fourth inning as host New York recorded a shutout over Tampa Bay in the opener of a day-night doubleheader.
With the victory, the Yankees temporarily prevented the Rays from clinching the AL East and moved six games ahead of the Boston Red Sox for the American League's top wild-card spot.
New York's Carlos Rodon (7-3) scattered three singles over eight innings as the Yankees finished off the victory in a brisk 2 hours, 2 minutes. Rodon struck out eight in his 100th career win and also reached 1,500 strikeouts for his career. Rays right-hander Nick Martinez (15-5) allowed two runs on five hits over six innings with seven strikeouts to take his first loss since July 9.
Dodgers 7, Padres 0
Freddie Freeman drove in three runs, Will Smith and Tommy Edman hit home runs, and Los Angeles inched closer to the best record in the National League with a shutout of visiting San Diego.
Eight Dodgers pitchers held down the red-hot Padres offense in a bullpen game, with Justin Wrobleski (12-5) earning the win. Roki Sasaki struck out two in one inning in his return from a blister issue. The Dodgers extended their home winning streak to 11 games.
Los Angeles moved to within one game of the NL-best Milwaukee Brewers and reduced its magic number for a top-two NL spot and a bye into the National League Division Series to one. Luis Campusano had two hits for the Padres, whose magic number to clinch a playoff spot remained at two.
Phillies 6, Brewers 4
Bryson Stott delivered the tiebreaking hit in the eighth inning to guide Philadelphia to a victory over visiting Milwaukee. Brandon Marsh homered and knocked in three runs as the Phillies lowered their magic number to two to clinch a postseason berth.
Zack Wheeler ended up with a no-decision after striking out 11 while giving up three runs and five hits in 5 2/3 innings. Wheeler struck out the first seven batters he faced, setting a Phillies record for consecutive strikeouts to begin a game. His first-inning strikeout of Brice Turang was the 2,000th of his career.
The Brewers saw their lead over the Dodgers for the top record in the majors shrink to one as they lost just the third time in their last 13 games. William Contreras knocked in three runs.
Marlins 8, Cubs 2 (12 innings)
Griffin Conine plated the go-ahead run that ignited a six-run 12th inning for visiting Miami, which snapped a three-game losing by beating Chicago and postponing the Cubs' playoff celebration for at least a day.
On a night when runs were scarce until the final inning, both teams endured a pair of scoreless extra frames before Conine broke the drought with a leadoff, golf-shot single off Caleb Thielbar that fell just inside the left field line. Esteury Ruiz, the automatic runner, scored from second to make it 3-2 as the Marlins sent 10 batters to the plate in the inning.
The Cubs could have clinched a wild-card playoff spot with a win or Arizona loss, but neither of those happened keeping the Diamondbacks mathematically alive. Josh Ekness (3-4) struck out a pair in the 11th inning to get the win while Thielbar (3-4) gave up three runs -- two earned -- in his inning of work.
Guardians 3, Red Sox 2
Nathaniel Lowe drove in Chase DeLauter with a sacrifice fly in the ninth inning and Cleveland held on to beat host Boston in the first game of a three-game series.
Cleveland not only extended its winning streak to six but maintained its one-game lead over the Chicago White Sox for first place in the AL Central.
Parker Messick held Boston to one run on five hits in five innings, his 14th straight start allowing three runs or fewer. Payton Tolle started for the Red Sox and gave up two runs on eight hits in 5 2/3 innings as the Guardians went 1-for-12 with runners in scoring position and stranded 15.
White Sox 14, Royals 11
Chase Meidroth smacked a three-run home run among his three hits and drove in five, and Brenton Doyle, Randal Grichuk and Munetaka Murakami also homered to power Chicago past host Kansas City.
Chicago won for the fourth time in five games to remain one game behind the AL Central-leading Cleveland Guardians. The White Sox, who hold the third and final AL wild-card spot, reduced their magic number to earn a playoff berth to three.
Vinnie Pasquantino hit a ninth-inning grand slam for the Royals, who lost their fifth straight. He went 3-for-5 with a double and also drove in five.
Nationals 3, Tigers 1
CJ Abrams hit a pair of home runs and drove in all three runs as visiting Washington topped Detroit. Abrams reached 100 RBIs for the season with his solo shot in the second inning, then broke a 1-1 tie in the seventh with his 33rd long ball of the season, a two-run blast.
Dylan Crews had two hits and scored the other run for the Nationals. Rookie Jackson Kent (2-4) earned the win in long relief. He allowed one run on six hits over four innings and struck out three. Opener Riley Cornelio lasted 2 2/3 innings, striking out four and walking three.
Ben Malgeri scored the Tigers' only run. Kevin McGonigle and Max Clark each had two hits.
Pirates 2, Cardinals 0
Jared Jones and two relievers combined on a one-hitter as Pittsburgh beat visiting St. Louis for a fifth straight win. Jones (5-6) lowered his ERA to 1.08 in four September starts and struck out nine with zero walks over seven innings while throwing 63 of his 86 pitches for strikes.
Pittsburgh broke a scoreless tie with two outs in the sixth inning on Ryan O'Hearn's RBI single against Andre Pallante (12-8). Pallante allowed one run on three hits with two walks and two strikeouts over six innings.
St. Louis struck out 14 times and lost for the fifth time in its last six games.
Astros 7, Mariners 0
Christian Walker hit a three-run home run, Yordan Alvarez launched a two-run homer and Isaac Paredes added a solo shot as Houston slugged and pitched its way past host Seattle.
Jose Altuve, Yainer Diaz, Alvarez and Paredes each collected two hits for the Astros, who pulled into a first-place tie with the Texas Rangers in the West. Five Astros pitchers combined to throw a four-hit shutout. Miguel Ullola (1-0) earned his first major league win, allowing one hit and striking out two over two innings of relief.
Julio Rodriguez notched two hits for Seattle. The Mariners went 0-for-3 with runners in scoring position and stranded nine.
Reds 4, Braves 0
Brandon Williamson fired six scoreless innings and Cincinnati supported him with three solo homers to defeat host Atlanta in the opener of a three-game series.
Cincinnati ended a two-game losing streak and evened the season series with Atlanta at 2-2. Williamson (5-4) worked six scoreless innings, allowing three hits and two strikeouts. Elly De La Cruz (29), Dane Myers (8) and Eugenio Suarez (25) each hit a home run for the Reds. It was Suarez's 350th career homer, making him the 10th active player to reach that mark.
Atlanta starter JR Ritchie (1-4) pitched five innings and allowed one run on four hits and three walks. The rookie struck out a career-high eight batters.
Mets 6, Rangers 3
Francisco Alvarez laced a go-ahead two-run double in the sixth, then scored an insurance run on an unusual sacrifice fly for visiting New York, who damaged Texas' playoff hopes with a win in the opener of a three-game interleague series in Arlington.
Juan Soto had an RBI single in the third, and Carson Benge capped the scoring with a run-scoring double in the seventh for the Mets. The club won hours after removing the interim tag from manager Andy Green and signing him to a three-year extension.
Josh Jung had an RBI double in the third, and Elias Diaz and Wyatt Langford lofted sacrifice flies in the fourth for the Rangers, who entered Tuesday with a one-game lead over the Houston Astros in the AL West.
Diamondbacks 7, Rockies 2
Nolan Arenado homered and doubled among his three hits, Michael Soroka tossed seven strong innings, and Arizona kept its slim postseason hopes alive with a win over host Colorado in Denver.
Geraldo Perdomo also had three hits and Ildemaro Vargas finished with two hits for Arizona, which remains alive in the NL wild-card race, sitting four games behind Philadelphia, San Diego and the Chicago Cubs for the third and final spot with five games to go.
Mickey Moniak homered for Colorado, which finished with just three hits and just one after the third inning. The Rockies (57-100) are the first team to lose 100 or more games in four straight seasons since the 1962-65 New York Mets.
Twins 3, Giants 2
Walker Jenkins homered, Luke Keaschall contributed both offensively and defensively, and Minnesota evened its road interleague series against San Francisco.
Taj Bradley (12-6) combined with four relievers on a six-hitter for the Twins, who used two late diving catches by Keaschall in right field to prevent the Giants from taking the first two of the series.
Bradley allowed just one other hit -- a fifth-inning single by Drew Gilbert -- in his six innings. He walked three and struck out six. Keaschall's one-out triple scored Ryan Kreidler, then Brooks Lee gave Minnesota the lead for good with a run-scoring single to plate Keaschall.
A's 9, Angels 7
Carlos Cortes hit a go-ahead two-run homer in the bottom of the eighth inning and the Athletics overcame a six-run deficit to beat Los Angeles in West Sacramento, Calif.
In addition to the homer off Sam Bachman, Cortes also delivered a pinch-hit RBI triple in the seventh, helping the Athletics end a six-game losing streak. Zack Gelof hit a two-run homer later in the eighth for the A's. Shea Langeliers and Lawrence Butler each had three hits and an RBI for the Athletics.
Denzer Guzman homered and drove in four RBIs for the Angels, who have lost four of their last six games. Mike Trout added three hits and two runs for Los Angeles (60-97), which has never lost 100 games in a season.

item.content:encoded:
In a change of direction, the New York Mets hired interim manager Andy Green for the full-time job on Tuesday, giving him a three-year contract.
The team made the announcement before starting its final road trip of the year with the opener of a three-game series in Texas against the Rangers.
“Over the course of the season, it became evident that the next manager of the New York Mets was already in place,” president of baseball operations David Stearns said in a statement. “Andy has demonstrated strong leadership qualities and a unique ability to forge connections with our emerging core and distinguished veterans. I look forward to continuing our great partnership as we turn toward the 2027 season.”
Green, who managed the San Diego Padres from 2016-19, had been running New York's farm system before taking over as interim manager when Carlos Mendoza was fired in late June. At the time, Green said he wasn't particularly interested in becoming a permanent skipper again, citing the desire to keep spending time with his three daughters and saying he viewed his interim role on the bench as more of a responsibility to the club than a personal opportunity.
Stearns said Green would return to a front-office role after the season, a stance the executive stuck to in the months that followed — even as the last-place Mets (71-85) improved on the field and several rookies who rose through the minors under Green such as Carson Benge and Nolan McLean flourished in the big leagues as well.
“The players in the clubhouse have rekindled the love I have for being in the dugout," Green said at a pregame news conference in Texas.
And in the end, the Mets committed to Green and chose not to conduct a full search for a new manager this offseason.
“I think Andy is the perfect person for this job,” Stearns said.
“Andy has connected with and pushed our players to perform, despite the disappointment of the season,” Mets owners Steve and Alex Cohen said in the statement. “Over the last several months he has brought discipline, accountability and positivity to the clubhouse, attributes we were seeking in our next manager. ... We are excited for his continued leadership in the dugout.”
Coming into the season, the Mets had high expectations for a franchise without a World Series title since 1986. New York opened the season with baseball’s highest payroll at $358 million and was projected to pay an additional $124 million in luxury tax.
But the Mets underperformed early and were beset by key injuries to Juan Soto, Francisco Lindor and others. They were 34-47 at the midpoint of the season when Mendoza was fired on June 26. The team is 37-38 since Green took over.
“The last three months I think there’s been progress,” Green said. “We’ve got more to do.”
The 49-year-old Green, a former major league infielder, went 274-366 as Padres manager and finished with a losing record in all four seasons. He joined the Mets in 2023 as senior vice president of baseball development and becomes the 26th manager in franchise history.
“I am excited and humbled to officially be named manager of the New York Mets,” Green said in the statement. “When I accepted the interim role, I didn’t anticipate it becoming permanent, but the more time I spent with our players and staff, the clearer it became that this is where my passion and experience could make the greatest impact. That realization led to many conversations with my family, and together we agreed this is the right opportunity at the right time.
"I want to thank Steve and Alex for the love, ambition and commitment with which they lead this organization, and David for the trust he has placed in me. I believe deeply in what we can build together, and I’m honored to continue serving our players, this organization and the amazing Mets fans.”

item.content:encoded:
After a 2025 offseason in which the Washington Nationals overhauled a ton of different things and processes within their organization, the club is back at it again. They hired President of Baseball Operations Paul Toboni to change the infrastructure at all levels, and he has now added another piece to his arsenal of brilliant minds.
Nationals poach new international scouting director from Astros
The Nationals continue to overhaul the organization's internal workings with another staffing change. This time, it's the acquisition of director of international scouting Brian Rodgers from the Houston Astros. The Athletic Nationals beat writer Spencer Nusbaum and Astros beat writer Chandler Rome were first with the news.
It's been a turbulent decade for Nationals international scouting. After Johnny DiPuglia took over in 2009, effectively starting from scratch having to clean up the complete mess Jim Bowden left the organization, they saw eventual success with talents like Juan Soto, Víctor Robles (though briefly), and Luis García Jr. That largely dried up later in the 2010s, with the team spending $3.9 million on Yasel Antuna, who crashed out of pro ball in 2023 after failing to produce at any level, in 2017.
In the 2019-20 signing period, the club gave out four bonuses of $600,000 or more to Andry Lara, Pablo Aldonis, Roismar Quintana, and Dawry Martinez. Only Lara ever made it to the big leagues, and while he's still on the 40-man roster, it's hard to imagine he'll maintain that status through 2027 without hitting outright waivers; his brief 9-game relief stint in 2025 was underwhelming, and he's got a 110 ERA- and 102 FIP- (where 100 is average and lower is better) at Rochester this year. Aldonis is still active but hasn't made it past Advanced-A as a 24-year-old. Quintana also never made it past Advanced-A before being released last year, and Martinez never even made it stateside before being cut from the org in 2023.
Other touted international signings since then have been equally underwhelming. Armando Cruz, given $3.9 million in 2021, never hit, and was cut as a 21-year-old last year. The next year, they gave Cristhian Vaquero $4.9 million, and he hasn't progressed past Advanced-A. He's got an 83 wRC+ in the lower minors this year. Nobody in the 2023 class has made any kind of splash in the system either. DiPuglia resigned in September of that year (though he joined the Royals four months later), beginning another period of internal turmoil in the team's international personnel department.
Fausto Severino was promoted from his longtime role as director of Latin American scouting to the international ops director for 2024. While 2024 is recent enough that it's hard to declare the top signing "busts," nobody from that signing class is in MLB Pipeline's Nationals top 30 prospect ranking. Neither Angel Feliz nor Victor Hurtado, the two seven-figure acquisitions, are in FanGraphs' top 45 for the organization. The club did not renew Severino's contract at year's end.
Victor Rodriguez took over as the director of international operations in 2025, overseeing a class that produced Marconi German. That was the only real acquisition that remains of note prior to Mike Rizzo's exit from the organization. Rodriguez remained in that role for the 2026 signing period, however, inking Samil Serrano, who ranked as MLB Pipeline's 26th overall international prospect. He's now the 16th-ranked player in the team's farm system.
Rodriguez will no longer serve in that role going forward, but will remain in the organization, Nusbaum and Rome's piece reports. A period from 2018 to 2024 of almost zero future major league talent being produced severely stunted the Nationals' lower minors, and new director Brian Rodgers is tasked with helping the organization continue to transform itself under the Toboni- and Kilambi-led regime. Rodgers had been Houston's international operations director since 2024, and his top signing of the 2025 international class, Kevin Alvarez, is the club's top-ranked prospect and sits at 77th overall on Pipeline's top 100.
It's one of many top-level changes being made in the Washington organization. Long-tenured director of medical services Harvey Sharman did not have his contract renewed for the 2027 season, Mark Zuckerman reported earlier this month. General manager Ani Kilambi told Nusbaum last week that the team intends to greatly expand its research & development department this offseason as well. It's certainly a new era of Nationals baseball. On this side of things, however, it's likely going to be a few years before we can measure any level of meaningful change.

item.content:encoded:
Mientras marchamos por la última semana de la temporada regular, no parece haber mucho suspenso respecto a quiénes serán nombrados JMV. Al menos, eso es lo que podemos descifrar de nuestra más reciente -- y última -- encuesta del JMV de MLB.com para el 2026.
El cubano Yordan Álvarez sigue estando bien al frente en la Liga Americana a pesar de una producción relativamente mediocre recientemente. En la Liga Nacional, Pete Crow-Armstrong está cerrando una de las mejores campañas completas en tiempos recientes.
Treinta y ocho expertos de MLB.com emitieron sus votos sobre quiénes creen que se llevarán los honores de JMV tras esta temporada, con 32 jugadores recibiendo al menos un voto. Como recordatorio, los votos se basaron no solo en el desempeño hasta ahora, sino también en cómo se espera que evolucionen las cosas durante el resto de la campaña.
Los votantes clasificaron a sus cinco principales candidatos de cada liga con un sistema de 5-4-3-2-1: cinco puntos por un voto al primer lugar, cuatro por el segundo, y así sucesivamente. Estos son los resultados.
Todas las estadísticas son hasta la jornada del domingo, a menos que se indique lo contrario.
LIGA AMERICANA
Álvarez ha tenido un desempeño tan bueno este año que lo que califica como un bache para él sería un gran trecho para la mayoría de los demás bateadores. En sus últimos 41 encuentros, batea .264 con OPS de .840. Reiteramos, nada mal para la mayoría, pero muy por debajo del nivel del líder de la Americana en promedio (.313) y OPS (1.027). Álvarez lleva tres cuadrangulares y cinco impulsadas a lo largo de 16 partidos este mes, dejándolo a un jonrón del dominicano Junior Caminero de los Rays por el liderato en el Joven Circuito y a seis empujadas de Pete Alonso por la cima en dicho departamento. Aunque sus posibilidades de la Triple Corona se están desvaneciendo un poco, Álvarez todavía ha armado un 2026 asombroso en el plato. Su wRC+ de 179 es al menos 27 puntos mejor que el de cualquier otro bateador calificado.
Sabemos que el quisqueyano es uno de los grandes cañoneros del juego. Está cerrando su segunda temporada consecutiva de 40 vuelacercas y está dando swings más fuerte que nadie. Pero lo que ha sido más impresionante de su temporada es su mejorado criterio en la zona de strike. Aumentó su tasa de boletos desde un 6.3% por debajo del promedio a un 11.5%, lo que se ubica en el 80mo percentil de MLB. También ha mantenido una tasa de ponches muy sólida (18.5%). Ya no persigue tantos pitcheos fuera de la zona, ha reducido su tasa de swings en blanco y está haciendo más contacto en general. Esa mezcla de paciencia, trueno y control del bate es una combinación especial, sobre todo en un jugador de 23 años. Luciendo un porcentaje de embasarse de .363 (52 puntos mejor que la campaña pasada), el OPS de .892 de Caminero se ubica tercero en la Americana.
Witt ha tenido mejores campañas a la ofensiva, aunque 18 bambinazos, 43 estafadas y wRC+ de 119 en 137 partidos no está nada mal. Pero cuando se consideran todas sus capacidades, Witt sigue siendo extremadamente valioso. Su valor de carreras defensivas de +16 está empatado en el tercer lugar de las Grandes Ligas, y sus 22 outs por encima del promedio encabezan la Liga Americana. También cuenta con un valor de carreras en el corrido de bases de +8, a uno de Corbin Carroll de los Diamondbacks por el liderato de MLB. Por eso, aunque no ha sido tan indiscutible en la caja de bateo como lo fue en el 2024 (wRC+ de 169), la grandeza integral de Witt lo tiene en la cima de la tabla de posiciones de WAR de FanGraphs en el Joven Circuito (6.6) y posiblemente perfilándolo entre los primeros cinco en la votación para JMV por tercera vez en tres años.
Ha habido bastante conversación de JMV entorno a Schlittler en las últimas semanas. ¿Y por qué no? Está marcando el paso en la Americana en efectividad (1.94), WHIP (0.91) y WAR de pitcheo de FanGraphs (6.1). Se ubica segundo en el Joven Circuito en promedio de bateo en contra (.182) y en tasa de ponches menos boletos (25.0%). Ha permitido una carrera o ninguna en 21 aperturas. Ese es un récord de la franquicia de los Yankees y algo que apenas otros dos lanzadores de 25 años o menos han logrado en la Era de la Pelota Viva (desde 1920): Blake Snell (2018) y Dean Chance (1964). Seguramente será reconocido con el Premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana a estas alturas, pero Schlittler recibirá su merecida cuota de consideración para el JMV.
Schlittler no ha sido el único miembro de los Bombarderos que ha sido indispensable este año. Mientras Nueva York ha estado sin Aaron Judge durante una gran parte de la campaña y ha echado de menos a otros bates estelares debido a lesiones, Rice ha sido demostrado consistencia. Se ubica tercero en el Joven Circuito en jonrones (39) y anotadas (100). Es cuarto en la liga en impulsadas (95) y OPS (.888), y está empatado en el cuarto lugar en valor de carreras al bate (+34). Con dos vuelacercas durante la última semana, Rice se convertiría en apenas el segundo miembro del equipo del Bronx diferente a Judge en la última década en conectar al menos 41 jonrones en una temporada, acompañando al dominicano Juan Soto (2024).
Otros que recibieron votos: El venezolano Willson Contreras, Medias Rojas; Pete Alonso, Orioles; Kevin McGonigle, Tigres; el cubano Miguel Vargas, Medias Blancas; el cubano Randy Arozarena, Marineros; Munetaka Murakami, Medias Blancas; Dylan Cease, Azulejos.
LIGA NACIONAL
El mes pasado, PCA dio el salto por encima de Ohtani hacia el puesto Nro. 1 de nuestra encuesta. Este mes, se ha apartado por completo del resto del grupo. Crow-Armstrong, quien recibió cada voto de primer lugar emitido por nuestro panel, está empatado con Kyle Schwarber en el liderato de bambinazos de MLB (45). Nadie tiene más anotadas (118), extrabases (83) o total de bases anotadas (351) esta campaña. Con 38 estafadas, el dinámico jardinero central del equipo del Norte de Chicago podría convertirse en el séptimo miembro del club 40-40 más adelante esta semana. Y no pase por alto el hecho de que es posiblemente el mejor jugador a la defensa en cualquier posición en estos momentos. Ya no es una cuestión de si Crow-Armstrong es el JMV de la Nacional. El premio es prácticamente suyo ahora mismo. Pero ¿lo ganará de manera unánime?
Ohtani se mantiene como el claro escolta en el Viejo Circuito a pesar de haber jugado en apenas tres partidos este mes debido a sus persistentes lesiones en la rodilla izquierda y el bíceps derecho. La buena noticia es que el dirigente de los Dodgers, Dave Roberts, dijo que "hay una buena posibilidad" de que Ohtani sea activado de la lista de lesionados de 15 días el miércoles tras cumplir la estadía mínima. No lanzará por el resto de la temporada, dejándolo con efectividad de 1.79 y 95 ponches en 85.2 entradas. Pero Ohtani tendrá unos cuantos partidos para sumar a sus totales ofensivos (30 jonrones, wRC+ de 142).
Mencionamos antes cómo Schlittler luce como el gran favorito para el Premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana. Misiorowski tendría su premio más asegurado en la Nacional. A lo largo de 169.1 episodios, Miz encabeza la Gran Carpa en casi cada categoría, incluyendo efectividad (1.86), WHIP (0.80), tasa de ponches menos boletos (31.7%) y fWAR (6.5), por nombrar solo algunas. Sus oponentes tienen un diminuto OPS de .474 contra Misiorowski, la segunda menor cifra para cualquier abridor calificado en la Era Divisional (desde 1969). Los oponentes del quisqueyano Pedro Martínez, en una de las mejores campañas para un lanzador, registraron OPS de .473 en el 2000.
El dominicano, quien no recibió un solo voto en nuestra anterior encuesta de JMV, ha estado encendido con Cincinnati durante el último mes. En sus últimos 27 encuentros, batea .404 con ocho vuelacercas, seis bases robadas y OPS de 1.205. Dio múltiples hits en 14 de esos partidos, y su fWAR de 2.5 durante este transcurso es el mejor de las Mayores. Esta prolongada racha encendida le ha dado a De la Cruz un wRC+ de 139 -- el mejor de su carrera -- y lo deja a dos jonrones más dos estafadas de convertirse en el cuarto jugador de los Rojos en el club 30-30 y el primero desde Brandon Phillips en el 2007.
Schwarber ha caído en un pequeño bache, bateando de 34-4 con un cuadrangular en sus últimos 10 encuentros. También está a ocho ponches de establecer un récord de ponches en una misma campaña. De todas maneras, hay que admirar la consistencia de Schwarber. Terminará con más de 40 vuelacercas y 150 juegos disputados en cuatro de las últimas cinco temporadas. Ha superado los 100 boletos negociados por cuarto año consecutivo, y un tercer título de bambinazos del Viejo Circuito está a su alcance.
Otros que recibieron votos: El dominicano Fernando Tatis Jr., Padres; Brice Turang, Cerveceros; Matt Olson, Bravos; James Wood, Nacionales; Jordan Walker, Cardenales; Alex Bregman, Cachorros; Bryce Harper, Filis; Jake Bauers, Cerveceros; el dominicano Otto López, Marlins; el venezolano Gabriel Moreno, Diamondbacks; el dominicano Rafael Devers, Gigantes; Alec Burleson, Cardenales; CJ Abrams, Nacionales; Corbin Carroll, Diamondbacks; el dominicano Cristopher Sánchez, Filis.

item.content:encoded:
As we make our way through the final week of the regular season, there doesn't seem to be much suspense as to who will be named MVP. At least, that's what we can glean from our latest -- and final -- MLB.com 2026 MVP poll.
Yordan Alvarez is still well out in front in the American League despite relatively mediocre production of late. In the National League, Pete Crow-Armstrong is wrapping up one of the best all-around seasons in recent memory.
Thirty-eight MLB.com experts cast votes for who they think will earn MVP honors after this season, with 32 players receiving at least one vote. As a reminder, votes were based not only on results so far, but also on how things are expected to play out the rest of the season.
Voters ranked their top five picks in each league on a 5-4-3-2-1 scale -- five points for a first-place vote, four points for a second-place vote and so on. Here are the results.
All stats are through Sunday unless otherwise noted.
AMERICAN LEAGUE
Alvarez has been so good this year that what qualifies as a slump for him would be a good stretch for most other hitters. Over his past 41 games, he is hitting .264 with an .840 OPS. Again, not bad for most, but well below the standard of the AL leader in average (.313) and OPS (1.027). Alvarez has three homers and five RBIs through 16 games this month, leaving him tied with the O's Pete Alonso and one home run behind the Rays' Junior Caminero for the AL lead and nine RBIs behind Alonso for the top spot in that statistic. Even though his Triple Crown chances have faded, Alvarez has still put together an awesome 2026 at the plate. His 179 wRC+ is at least 27 points better than any other qualified hitter.
We know Caminero is one of the game's great sluggers. He is finishing up his second straight 40-homer season and swings harder than anyone. But what's been most impressive about his season is his improved strike-zone judgment. He has upped his walk rate from a below-average 6.3% to 11.5%, which ranks in the 80th percentile of MLB. He's also maintained a very solid strikeout rate (18.5%). He's not chasing as much, has shaved his whiff rate and is making more contact overall. That blend of patience, power and bat control is a special combination, especially in a 23-year-old player. Carrying a .363 on-base percentage (52 points better than last season), Caminero's .892 OPS ranks third in the AL.
Witt has had better offensive seasons, although 18 homers, 43 steals and a 119 wRC+ in 137 games is not too shabby. But when you consider his entire skill set, Witt remains extremely valuable. His +16 fielding run value is tied for third in the Majors, and his 22 outs above average tops the AL. He also has a +8 baserunning run value, one behind the D-backs' Corbin Carroll for the MLB lead. So while he hasn't been as undeniable in the batter's box as he was in 2024 (169 wRC+), Witt's all-around greatness has him atop the AL FanGraphs WAR leaderboard (6.6) and in line for a possible top-five finish in the MVP voting for the third time in three years.
There has been quite a bit of MVP chatter surrounding Schlittler in recent weeks. And why not? He is pacing the AL in ERA (1.94), WHIP (0.91) and FanGraphs pitching WAR (6.1). He ranks second in the junior circuit in opponents' batting average (.182) and strikeout-minus-walk rate (25.0%). He has allowed one or zero runs in 21 starts. That's a Yankees franchise record and something only two other pitchers age-25 or younger have accomplished in the Live Ball Era (since 1920): Blake Snell (2018) and Dean Chance (1964). He seems like a lock for the AL Cy Young Award at this point, but Schlittler will receive his fair share of MVP love.
Schlittler hasn't been the only indispensable Yankee this year. While New York has been without Aaron Judge for a large portion of the season and has missed other star bats as well due to injuries, Rice has been a constant. He ranks third in the AL in homers (39) and runs scored (100). He's fourth in the league in RBIs (95) and OPS (.888), and tied for fourth in batting run value (+34). With two homers during the final week, Rice would become just the second non-Judge Yankee over the past decade to hit at least 41 homers in a season, joining Juan Soto (2024).
Others receiving votes: Willson Contreras, Red Sox; Pete Alonso, Orioles; Kevin McGonigle, Tigers; Miguel Vargas, White Sox; Randy Arozarena, Mariners; Munetaka Murakami, White Sox; Dylan Cease, Blue Jays
NATIONAL LEAGUE
Last month, PCA jumped over Ohtani and into the No. 1 spot in our poll. This month, he has run away from the rest of the field. The recipient of every first-place vote cast by our panel, Crow-Armstrong is tied with Kyle Schwarber for the MLB lead in home runs (45). No one has more runs (118), extra-base hits (83) or total bases (351) this season. With 38 steals, the Cubs' dynamic center fielder could become the seventh member of the 40-40 club later this week. Oh, and let's not overlook the fact that he is arguably the best defensive player at any position right now. It's no longer a question of whether Crow-Armstrong is the NL MVP. The award is as good as his right now. But will he win it in unanimous fashion?
Ohtani remains the clear runner-up in the NL despite playing in just three games this month due to his nagging left knee and right biceps injuries. The good news is Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said "there's a good chance" Ohtani will be activated from the 15-day injured list Wednesday after a minimum stint. He won't pitch for the rest of the season, leaving him with a 1.79 ERA and 95 K's over 85 2/3 innings. But Ohtani will have a few games to add to his offensive totals (30 homers, 142 wRC+).
We mentioned earlier how Schlittler looks like the heavy favorite for the AL Cy Young Award. Misiorowski is an even bigger shoo-in in the senior circuit. Through 169 1/3 innings, Miz leads the Majors in just about every category, including ERA (1.86), WHIP (0.80), strikeout-minus-walk rate (31.7%) and fWAR (6.5), to name just a few. Opposing batters have a scant .474 OPS against Misiorowski, which is the second-lowest by any qualified starter in the Divisional Era (since 1969). Pedro Martinez, in one of the greatest seasons by a pitcher, recorded a .473 opponents' OPS in 2000.
De La Cruz, who didn't receive a single vote in our previous MVP poll, has been red-hot for Cincinnati over the past month. In his last 27 games, he is batting .404 with eight homers, six steals and a 1.205 OPS. He collected multiple hits in 14 of those games, and his 2.5 fWAR during this period is the best in the big leagues. This prolonged hot streak has given De La Cruz a career-best 139 wRC+ and has left him two homers and two steals away from becoming the fourth Red in the 30-30 club and the first since Brandon Phillips in 2007.
Schwarber has fallen into a bit of a rut, going 4-for-34 with one home run over his past 10 games. He's also eight strikeouts away from setting a new record for K's in a single season. Even so, you have to admire Schwarber's consistency. He will end up with more than 40 homers and 150 games played in four of the past five seasons. He has surpassed 100 walks for a fourth consecutive season, and a third NL home run title is right there for the taking, too.
Others receiving votes: Fernando Tatis Jr., Padres; Brice Turang, Brewers; Matt Olson, Braves; James Wood, Nationals; Jordan Walker, Cardinals; Alex Bregman, Cubs; Bryce Harper, Phillies; Jake Bauers, Brewers; Otto Lopez, Marlins; Gabriel Moreno, Diamondbacks; Rafael Devers, Giants; Alec Burleson, Cardinals; CJ Abrams, Nationals; Corbin Carroll, Diamondbacks; Cristopher Sánchez, Phillies

Juan Soto Joins Elite Club With 270 Homers, 100 Stolen Bases Before 28th Birthday
New York Mets outfielder Juan Soto just became the fourth player in MLB history to hit 270 home runs and steal 100 bases before his 28th birthday. Friday night, the…
Juan Soto of the New York Mets hits a double in the second inning against the Philadelphia Phillies at Citi Field on September 18, 2026 in New York City.
Photo by Evan Bernstein/Getty Images
New York Mets outfielder Juan Soto just became the fourth player in MLB history to hit 270 home runs and steal 100 bases before his 28th birthday. Friday night, the 27-year-old crushed a 428-foot three-run blast against the Philadelphia Phillies.
Who else made this list? Alex Rodriguez, Ken Griffey Jr., and Mike Trout, per MLB's Sarah Langs. Every player in this group debuted at 19.
According to Essentially Sports, Soto went 3-for-5 with one homer, 3 RBIs, and a run scored against Philadelphia. He's up to 26 homers in 103 games despite missing time on the injured list twice this year.
The five-time All-Star needed 1,199 MLB games to reach 270 home runs. He's also collected 210 doubles as part of his 1,187 hits.
The Dominican star has swiped 104 bases in 134 tries. Last season, he stole 38 bags—a massive jump from his previous career-high of just 12. This year he's 9-for-12 on the basepaths.
Soto draws walks like few others can. He's led MLB in walks four times and has six seasons with at least 100 free passes. Career totals? 969 walks versus only 893 strikeouts. Among active players, he leads everyone with a .415 on-base percentage.
New York inked the outfielder as a free agent before the 2025 season. His contract: 15 years, $765 million. That's the biggest deal in MLB history.
The Mets sit in last place in the NL East at 70-84. Many experts predicted they'd contend for the division title this year. They haven't.
Soto's still producing. He's batting .274 with a .920 OPS across 444 plate appearances in 103 games. His season started late on April 22 after he recovered from a right calf strain. Then he hit the IL again in late July with a left calf strain. He earned his fifth All-Star selection this season but didn't play in the game.
